title: The Reindeer With the First Snow
creature: A reindeer who brings the first snow down
summary: He has been late three years running, and the herders have stopped pretending not to notice.

chapters.title: Coming Down
chapters.text: The herd on the Cairngorms is free-ranging over about four hundred hectares of the high plateau and it comes down to the enclosure at Glenmore when it wants to, which is mostly in the winter, and there is nothing at all mysterious about that. There is grazing up there in summer and there is not much in December. Reindeer are extremely good at digging for lichen through snow and extremely bad at coping with the wet warm winters that part of Scotland has been getting, and when the tops go hard they come down and the herders put food out and everybody is happy. That is what the visitors are told and it is true. Morag has said it perhaps two thousand times. It is on a laminated card and it is in the talk and it is what she tells the families who come up the hill in waterproofs in July to see reindeer in a Scottish summer and are usually surprised by how much they smell. What Morag was told, by her mother, who has worked with that herd since 2004, is the other thing. The herd comes down when it likes. Some of them come down in October and some hang about until January and there is no order to it that anybody has ever been able to chart. Except the bull. There is one bull — his name in the herd book is a number and the herders call him something else that Morag is not going to write down, because that name is theirs and she does not think it belongs in a story — and he comes down alone, ahead of everything, in a straight line off the Cairn Lochan side. And it snows within about thirty hours. Morag grew up with this the way other children grow up with a family saying. Her mother would come in and take her boots off and say *he's down*, and Morag's father would look at the window, and there would be snow on the tops by the following afternoon, and nobody ever remarked on it because remarking on it would have been like remarking that the kettle had boiled. Not sometimes. Every year that anybody in that family has kept track of, and Morag's mother has kept track since 2004 in a notebook that also has feed orders and a recipe for flapjack in it. Twenty-one years. Twenty-one first snows on the plateau, twenty-one bulls walking down off Cairn Lochan somewhere between one and thirty hours before, and eighteen of them accurate to within a day. It is not always the same animal. That is the part visitors get stuck on and that Morag's mother is brisk about: a bull is good for perhaps eleven or twelve years and there have been four of them in twenty-one, and each one has done it, and nobody taught them, and there is no lineage — the current one is not the son of the last. What there is, as far as anybody in that family can see, is a plateau, and a set of conditions on it, and whichever animal happens to be the one that notices first.

chapters.title: The Three
chapters.text: The three that are not are 2022, 2023 and 2024. In 2022 he came down on the fourth of November and the first lying snow on the plateau was on the nineteenth. In 2023 he came down on the ninth of November and the snow came on the twenty-eighth. In 2024 he came down on the second and the snow came on the sixth of December, which is thirty-four days, which is not a margin of error. It is a different month. Morag's mother wrote all three of those in the notebook without any note attached. Fourth of November, fifteen days. Ninth of November, nineteen days. Second of November, thirty-four days. She has never underlined anything in that book and she did not start. Morag was eleven in 2024 and she was in the enclosure with her mother on the afternoon he came down and she said, before she thought about it, "He's wrong again." Her mother did not answer for a while and then said: "He's not wrong." Morag said that thirty-four days was wrong. And her mother — who is not a sentimental person and who has spent twenty-one years putting food out for animals in horizontal rain and has views about people who anthropomorphise them — said: "He came down when the tops stopped being worth staying on. That is the only thing he has ever done. He has never once been telling us about the weather." Morag remembers exactly where they were standing and that it was raining and that her mother said it without any heat at all, in the voice she uses for saying that a gate is broken. Morag said that if that was true then the eighteen years were a coincidence. Her mother said no. She said that the tops stopping being worth staying on and the first snow used to be the same event, and that they are not the same event any more, and that this is the whole of it and there is nothing else in it.

chapters.title: The Notebook
chapters.text: Morag did the arithmetic that winter because she wanted her mother to be wrong. She had twenty-one years of her mother's notebook — the date he came down, in her mother's handwriting, in among the feed orders — and she got the snow dates from the weather station at Cairngorm summit, which has been recording since 1977 and which is public and which anybody can download. She was expecting to find that the gap was noise. Eighteen good years and three bad ones is exactly what a coincidence looks like, and she was twelve by then and had done a term of statistics and was extremely pleased with herself about it. The plan, which she had thought about for a week and which she still thinks was a reasonable plan, was to show her mother a scatter plot with no trend in it and say *there*. The gap is not noise. It is a trend. It is not a dramatic one and it does not go up in a straight line, and there are two years in the middle where it goes backwards. But you can put a line through those twenty-one points and the line has a slope, and the slope says that the interval between him coming down and the snow arriving has been getting longer by a bit under a day a year since about 2011. She checked it against the summit temperature series and got the thing she was not looking for, which is that the two lines are the same shape. She would like to be clear about the limits of this. It is twenty-one points. It is one bull at a time on one plateau, and the come-down dates were written by one woman who was mainly writing about feed, and Morag was twelve and taught herself the regression off the internet. She has since had it looked at by a teacher who does statistics properly and who was kind about it and who said the sample was small, the effect was real, and the conclusion was correct for reasons that had almost nothing to do with the reindeer — because the summit temperature series alone says the same thing on its own without any animals in it at all. He is not late. That is what Morag understood, sitting on the floor with a laptop in the January she was twelve, and it took her about a fortnight to stop feeling sick about it. The fortnight is worth explaining because she was not upset about the climate, which she had known about since she was seven and which is on the news. What got her was smaller and more specific. For eighteen years there had been an arrangement — an animal came down a hill and the weather did a thing — and it had been in her family and in that notebook and nobody had built it or maintained it and it had simply been true. And it had stopped being true during her own childhood, quietly, in three years, without anybody doing anything wrong. He is doing exactly what he has always done, on exactly the same cue, at more or less the same point in the autumn. The lichen goes, and the ground gets soft and sour, and a bull who has been on that plateau for eleven years decides it is not worth it any more and walks down off Cairn Lochan in a straight line the way he has every year of his life. The snow is what has moved.

chapters.title: What They Tell Visitors
chapters.text: Morag is fifteen and she works weekends at the enclosure in the summer and she is very good with the visitors, everybody says so. She tells them the true and cheerful things. That reindeer hooves spread in summer and harden in winter. That they are the only deer where the females keep antlers through the winter, which is why every Christmas card in Britain is wrong. That this herd came from Sweden in 1952 and that the man who brought them was called Mikel Utsi and that the first three arrived by boat. She tells them that reindeer can see ultraviolet, which is genuinely the best fact on the hill and which stops a group of eight-year-olds dead every single time. Snow reflects UV and lichen absorbs it, and so does fur, and so does urine, which means that a landscape that looks blank white to a person is, to a reindeer, covered in writing. She does not tell them about the bull. It is not a secret and there is no rule about it and if a visitor asked her directly she would answer honestly, and one man did, in 2026, who turned out to know a great deal about herds in Norway, and she talked to him for forty minutes. He said that the same argument was going on in three places in Finnmark and that nobody there had twenty-one years of dates either, because the people who know are herders and herders write down what they need and nothing else. He gave her an email address and she has not used it, and it is in the front of her mother's notebook on a piece of card. The reason she does not tell them is that it does not work as a nice fact. Every other thing she says on that hill can be said in a cheerful voice to a family with a four-year-old. *He comes down and it snows within thirty hours* is a wonderful one — it is the best one she has — and it was true for eighteen years and she cannot say it any more without saying the rest. And the rest is: he still comes down, and he is still right about the plateau, and the plateau is not what it was, and the notebook her mother keeps with the flapjack recipe in it is now a record of something nobody set out to record. Her mother has kept it up. Twenty-third of November 2025, thirty-one days. She writes it in the same handwriting in among the feed orders and does not comment. Morag has asked her twice whether she is going to send it to anybody. Her mother says she is a herder and not a scientist and that the notebook is for the feed, and that if somebody wants it after she is finished with it they are welcome to it, and that in the meantime there are animals to see to. Morag has a copy. She made it at fourteen, over about six evenings, photographing every page on her phone, and she has it in two places and one of them is not in that house. She did not ask permission and she did not hide it either. Her mother came in halfway through the third evening, looked at what she was doing, said nothing whatsoever, and put the kettle on. That is the only conversation the two of them have ever had about whether the notebook matters, and Morag thinks it was a fairly complete one.
